summary: H.R. 1534, known as the IMPACT Act, requires the Department of Energy to create a temporary, seven-year program focused on the research, development, demonstration, and commercial application of advanced production techniques for low-emissions cement, concrete, and asphalt.

affected_groups.effect: May apply for and receive funding to carry out demonstration projects, research, and technical assistance.
affected_groups.group: Eligible entities (institutions of higher education, state and federal entities, nonprofit research institutions, privat

affected_groups.effect: Must establish, coordinate, and oversee the research program, strategic plans, demonstration projects, and technical assistance.
affected_groups.group: Department of Energy and other federal agencies

key_provisions: Establishes a temporary research, development, and demonstration program at the Department of Energy for low-emissions cement, concrete, and asphalt production.
Requires the Secretary of Energy to develop a 5-year strategic plan for the program and submit updates every two years to Congress.
Focuses on specific areas including carbon capture, alternative fuels, energy efficiency, high-performance computing, sensor technologies, and retrofitting existing plants.
Directs the Department of Energy to support demonstration projects in collaboration with other agencies, industry partners, and universities, prioritizing regional and technological diversity.
Establishes a technical assistance program to help eligible entities with activities like data collection, life-cycle assessments, and updating standards.
Terminates the program seven years after enactment.
missing_information: Specific funding amounts or appropriations authorized by the bill.
Specific criteria for how entities are chosen for funding beyond broad categories like regional and technological diversity.
summary_detail.plain_summary: H.R. 1534, known as the IMPACT Act, requires the Department of Energy to create a temporary, seven-year program focused on the research, development, demonstration, and commercial application of advanced production techniques for low-emissions cement, concrete, and asphalt.
summary_detail.significance: The bill directs federal resources toward altering how fundamental construction materials like cement, concrete, and asphalt are produced. The significance depends on the scale of funding allocated, the success of the demonstration projects, and whether advanced low-emissions production methods become commercially viable at a comparable price to traditional methods.
